About

Hi! I’m Jordan, and I am a junior at San Diego State University studying aerospace engineering. Over the past 3 years, I have developed expertise in aerodynamics and propulsion, applying them to create functional prototypes and lead collaborative projects that deliver real results.

Outside the classroom, I expand my engineering skills through the Rocket Project club, working across various launch vehicle designs. Starting in the solid fuels section of the club, I grew my understanding of airframe structures and in-flight control systems. Now, I pass on the knowledge I have learned to new members and mentor them throughout the build processes.

On the bench 2

Queen Caline

In design

Solo build · 54 mm minimum diameter · K class solid · target December 2026

Queen Caline is a minimum-diameter build designed to achieve supersonic speeds. At minimum diameter, fin integrity becomes the critical point of failure for this flight. Since the entire lower airframe is displaced by the motor, the structure leaves the fins bonded to the airframe skin, creating extreme vulnerability to dynamic pressure and ultimately flutter velocity thresholds.

The rocket’s model main focus is to keep in mind the stresses it will experience while approaching the Mach 1.42 target. In places such as choosing the sleek von Kármán nose cone and reinforcing the beveled fins with a composite layup, Queen Caline maximizes its ability to handle drag and flutter throughout the flight.

At the heart of Queen Caline is the avionics bay. This section houses two flight computers, Blue Raven 2 (primary) and Easy Mini (redundant), to determine where the rocket is in flight and when to deploy the recovery parachutes. A stripped GoPro camera lens is also equipped to record Queen Caline’s ascent to the sky, removing the bulky housing and interfaces from 119g to just 18g!

Performance 2

Project lead

Rocket Project SDSU, Solid Fueled Rocketry Section · two stage · launch 13 December 2026

Performance 2 is classified as sub-minimum diameter as the motor subassembly is now the same diameter as the airframe itself. Joined by a coupler, the two components become fastened together through a centering rod, ultimately leaving the load path to run through the casing instead of around it.

The current model is set to fly on an L1000W for the sustainer and an M1850W for the booster. In the actual flight, the first stage of the whole rocket vehicle is predicted to reach a top speed of Mach 1.6. After burnout of the first stage and some time, Performance 2 will undergo a controlled separation, igniting the second-stage sustainer in the process to ultimately continue to an apogee of 51,000ft at a max velocity of Mach 3.18. Again, the critical points of failure for Performance 2 are the fin cans with dynamic pressure and flutter velocity, which provided the strict criteria for fin form and anchoring.

With the team, I am leading the development of the design and build. I manage the timeline of production against a fixed launch date and organize scheduled meetings and build days. Within these times, I oversee 6 members in their subsections of avionics and structures, mentoring and guiding them when needed.

Katana

Recovery

Katana was an Apogee Components 54 mm motor kit on a 4 in airframe, carrying an onboard camera. It was modeled in OpenRocket before the flight and reached roughly 2,300 ft, close to what the model predicted.

Avionics

Recovery was electronic dual deployment. I packed my own ejection charges and fired them from a Blue Raven 2, so the motor delay grain was not the trigger and the altimeter had full authority over both events.

The flight

Before flying it I pop tested the ejection charges on the ground. They fired and pulled the chute clear, so the charges and the electronics were not the open question going into the flight.

The vehicle reached altitude as intended. The recovery did not. The nose cone never separated, so the parachute never came out.

Failure analysis, three contributing causes

  1. The ejection charge was undersized for the volume it had to pressurize.
  2. The nose cone fit too tightly to the body tube, so the separation force needed was higher than designed for.
  3. The vent hole sat too close to the charge, bleeding pressure out of the bay at the moment it needed to build.

Any one alone might have been survivable. Together they removed the margin entirely. All three are packaging and sizing decisions rather than component failures, which is why the Queen Caline recovery bay is being laid out against them explicitly.

The vehicle

Encore was a two stage solid fueled rocket built by a team of eight and launched in May 2026. My part of it was the avionics bay.

The bay

I owned the bay end to end: designing it, fitting the components, and testing them before flight. It had to live inside a fixed spacing and a fixed available volume set by the rest of the airframe, so packaging drove component selection as much as function did.

Testing

Testing was the part that mattered most. An avionics bay that fits and does not fire is worse than one that never got built, so every component was verified in the assembled stack rather than on the bench alone.

Launch day

Eight of us put it on the pad in May 2026.

The build

ARCAS was my first high power vehicle, built from an Apogee Components kit with a 2.64 in body and a 29 mm motor mount. Because it was a kit rather than a clean sheet design, the work was in the build and the flight readiness check rather than in simulation.

The vehicle

Stability was verified by locating the center of gravity against the center of pressure and confirming the margin before it went on the rail.

The flight

It flew to 1,500 ft on single deployment and was the flight that earned my high power certification.
